subtype: Approach: trying to time the market [Pitfall]

Nikita's diary, 12 November.
In April, when the market fell, I stopped my monthly investment. My plan was simple: wait for the bottom, then buy back in cheaper. Pranav at work said, "Nobody knows where the bottom is." I thought I was smarter than that.
In May it dropped a little more, and I thought, wait, it'll go lower. In June it bounced. I thought, that's a fake bounce, it'll fall again. By August it was higher than when I stopped. I told myself I'd buy on the next dip.
There was a dip in September, a small one. I waited for a bigger one. It never came. Tonight I checked: the market is fifteen percent above where it was in April. Seven months of instalments I never made are sitting in my savings account.
I didn't lose money, exactly. I just missed everything.

qa.a: In April, when the market fell.

qa.a: Nikita feels regretful and a bit foolish, having missed the whole rebound while waiting.

subtype: Approach: rebalancing by written rule [Action]
passage:
Siddharth Mama took a folded paper from his old wallet when Ira asked how he had stayed calm in crashes. "I wrote this at twenty-five, after my first job. 'Seventy percent in shares, thirty in safe deposits. If either side drifts more than five points, move it back. Check once a year, in March.' That's all.
The first test came two years later. The market crashed. My share part had dropped to sixty percent. Every newspaper said sell. My heart said sell. But the paper said: move money from the safe side into shares, back to seventy. So I did, in small steps, over two months. It felt terrible, like throwing money into a fire.
Three years later, that was the best money I ever put in. Not because I was clever. Because I decided when I was calm, and obeyed the paper when I was scared."

qa.q: When did Siddharth check his mix each year?
qa.a: Once a year, in March.

qa.q: How did young Siddharth feel moving money into shares during the crash?
qa.a: It felt terrible, like throwing money into a fire; he was frightened but followed his written rule.

qa.q: Which choice in the story mattered most, and why?
qa.a: Writing the rule when calm and following it when scared, because it stopped fear from making the decision.

qa.q: What would have changed if he had followed the newspapers?
qa.a: He would likely have sold near the bottom and missed what became his best investment.

grounding: It shows a young investor following a rule written in calm times, moving a small share from safe deposits back into shares when the mix drifts during a crash.

Farida's rule sat in a note on her phone, written two years earlier with help from Amandeep, a friend who was a registered adviser: "Target 60% shares, 40% debt funds. If shares drift below 55% or above 65%, move back to 60. Only on the first working day of a quarter."
On 1 April the market had fallen hard, and her share portion had slipped to 52 percent. The complication: Farida was at a client site in rural Odisha for two weeks, with one bar of signal and a laptop that kept dying.
She could have waited until she got back, when things looked calmer. Instead, at 6 am, standing on the guest-house roof where the signal was best, she moved enough from her debt fund into shares to bring it back to 60. It took twenty minutes and three dropped connections.
She didn't look at the market again until July.

Bhupen worked night shifts at a call centre in Guwahati, and during the market fall his phone never left his hand. Between calls he refreshed his investment app, market channels and three groups that posted red charts. On bad nights he checked forty times. He slept badly, and twice he nearly sold everything at 4 am.
His flatmate Ayesha watched him check the app during dinner one weekend. "Does looking make it go up?"
He thought about it later on the bus home. "Every time I check, I get scared. When I'm scared, I want to do something. And the something is usually selling." The checking wasn't information. It was fuel.
So he made a rule: portfolio check on the first Sunday of each month, nothing else. He muted the market channels and left two of the groups. The first week his thumb kept reaching for the app out of habit. By the third week, the urge to sell had almost gone.

qa.a: On the first Sunday of each month.

In his shared flat in Bengaluru, Thomas noticed a pattern in March. Every time he checked his portfolio, which was about every hour, his chest tightened and he opened the sell screen. Twice he closed it at the last second. His colleague Mridul laughed when Thomas showed him his phone's screen-time report: two hours a day on market apps and channels.
That night Thomas worked it out on the balcony. "The price moves whether I look or not. Looking only changes me. And the more I look, the more I want to act, and my urges have been bad ideas."
So he set a rule: a portfolio check once a month, on the first Saturday, with a cup of tea. He muted two market channels, unfollowed the loudest accounts and moved the investment app into a folder on his last screen.
By April his time on market apps was ten minutes a week. The market was still wobbly. He wasn't.

At the co-operative bank branch in the small town of Karad, Rafiq leaned over Aadhya's desk at lunch. "Listen. That cement company's share has fallen sixty percent. My cousin in Mumbai says it will double by Diwali. Put something in now, before everyone else does."
Aadhya had ₹1.5 lakh saved for her sister's wedding. Rafiq sounded so sure. That evening, without reading anything about the company, she put in a lakh.
For two weeks the price went up a little, and she felt clever. Then it fell. And fell. In December the newspaper said the company had defaulted on its loans; it owed far more than it could pay, and had for months. The share was worth almost nothing.
Rafiq avoided her in the canteen. Aadhya sat on the bus home doing the maths again and again, wondering how to tell her mother about the wedding money.

Ingrid had been saving for a flat deposit. She didn't read the company's reports; they looked long and dull. She moved half her savings into the stock the next morning and texted Esther a thumbs-up.

When the market fell twenty percent in October, Leela felt the old panic rising in her Hyderabad flat. Then she remembered: two years ago it had fallen twelve percent, and she had written notes.
She found the file on her laptop. "Date: March. Down 12%. Felt like selling everything. Didn't. Recovered by September." And underneath, in capitals: "MY TECH FUND FELL TWICE AS MUCH AS EVERYTHING ELSE. I DIDN'T KNOW I HAD SO MUCH IN ONE SECTOR."
She read it twice. The first part told her to stay with the plan. The second told her what to change. She checked: tech was again nearly half her portfolio. That evening she called her friend Nilesh, who had studied finance, to talk it through, and booked a session with a registered adviser. She kept her monthly plan running, and after the adviser meeting she moved part of the tech fund into a broader fund.
In her notes she added a new line: "October. Down 20%. Stayed. Spread out."

qa.a: That it fell twice as much as everything else, and that she hadn't known she had so much in one sector.

qa.q: How did Leela feel when the market fell in October?
qa.a: Leela felt the old panic rising, until her notes steadied her.

In Hubli, Ishita's investments had been chosen for her by a relative two years earlier, and when the market fell she realised she couldn't explain any of them. Her colleague Mohit at the district co-operative office mentioned a registered adviser who charged a fixed fee per session, had a small office above a sweet shop on the main road, and sold no products.
She went on a Saturday with her statements in a plastic folder and a list of questions in Kannada and English. The adviser spent an hour explaining, in general, what each fund held, how risk and time usually relate, and what choices people in her position often consider. When Ishita asked, "So what should I do?", the adviser smiled. "Let's first make sure you understand the options. Then you decide, and come back if you want."
She walked home past the sweet shop feeling, for the first time, that her money made sense.

On a Sunday afternoon in her Chennai flat, Arohi finally sat down with the question Karthik had asked her at work: "If you lost your job tomorrow, how long could you last?"
She didn't know. So she wrote it out. Her share of the rent. Food. The two-wheeler EMI. The money she sends Amma every month. Phone and travel. She added up the fixed costs and left out things she could cut, like eating out.
Then she thought it through aloud. "Job searches take months. Karthik's took five. So six months of this is my number." She multiplied and circled it. It looked huge.
"But I don't need it tomorrow," she said. "If I build it over two years..." She divided the target by twenty-four and wrote the answer on a sticky note: the monthly goal. It was a real number, but one she could reach. She stuck it on her laptop.

qa.a: Five months.

qa.q: How did Arohi feel when she circled the six-month total?
qa.a: It looked huge and a little daunting, until splitting it into a monthly goal made it feel reachable.

qa.a: Those could be cut in an emergency, so the target reflects what she truly has to pay each month.

For two years I told myself I'd save whatever was left. Every month, around the 25th, there was nothing left. Not because I was reckless; small things just fill any empty space.
Yusuf, my flatmate, had a different system. By the evening his salary came in, a fixed amount had already gone into savings at another bank. "I never see it," he said. "So I never miss it."
In July I finally did the same. Twenty minutes on the bank's website: a standing instruction for the 1st of every month, the day my salary lands, into a savings account I have no card for.
The first month I noticed it. By the third, I didn't. Last week I checked the other account. Six months of transfers, and I had never once had to decide to save.

Employee wellness coach's note, 5 August.
Yogesh, from the logistics team, came to the money-habits session and admitted he had tried to save by willpower three times this year. Each time, by the 20th, the money was gone.
Instead of a budget talk, we did one thing. He logged into his bank on his phone and, with me beside him, set a standing instruction: a fixed amount moves into a separate savings account on the 1st, the day his salary arrives. He chose an amount he said wouldn't hurt, and he chose not to link that account to his debit card.

Follow-up, 5 November: three transfers done, none reversed. He said the best part was not having to fight himself every month.

Akash worked at the tea factory office in Munnar, and every year when appraisals came round he told his colleague Elizabeth the same thing: "Next year, after the raise, I'll start saving properly."
Each raise came. Each time, something grew to meet it: a better phone, a bike loan, weekend trips to Kochi with friends. His account still ran close to empty by the end of every month.
In the monsoon his father slipped on the wet estate path and broke his hip. The small hospital in town sent him on to a bigger one in Kottayam. The bill for surgery and ten days' stay came to more than Akash earned in three months. His father's small insurance covered only part.
Akash had nothing put aside. He borrowed from Elizabeth, from his uncle, from a moneylender his father had warned him about. Sitting on the hospital bench at night, he did the sums again and again. "After the raise," he said quietly to himself, "was always one year away."

Maria's company health cover would end in ten days when she switched jobs, and the new employer's cover wouldn't start for three months. The sales calls began at once. One agent rang four times, promising "best plan, everything covered, sign today".
Instead of signing, Maria made a checklist with her friend Sarika, who had once had a claim rejected: cover amount, waiting periods for existing conditions, room rent limit, exclusions, and each insurer's record of settling claims.
With the clock ticking, they split the work. Sarika pulled the claim-settlement figures from the regulator's published reports. Maria downloaded four policy documents and read the exclusions section of each, even though it made her eyes ache.
The "everything covered" plan had a room-rent limit so low that a normal hospital room would mean paying the difference herself. Another had a four-year waiting period. On day eight, Maria chose the third plan, with a higher premium but fewer traps, and paid online before the deadline.

passage:
Sudha's parents in Pune had never had health insurance, and after her father's short hospital stay last year, she decided to buy a family policy herself. Her colleague Aditi forwarded an ad: "Cheapest cover in India!"
Sudha didn't click it. That evening at her desk in the Hinjewadi office, she made a table with five columns: cover amount, waiting period for existing illnesses, room rent limit, exclusions, and how reliably each insurer pays claims. Then she filled it in for five insurers, reading each policy's fine print instead of the brochure.
The cheapest one excluded anything related to her father's blood pressure for four years. Another capped room rent so low that most private rooms would cost extra. By Friday, two policies were left. She sent the table to Aditi.
"I'd never have noticed the waiting period," Aditi wrote back. "Can I use your table?"

qa.a: Five columns.

qa.q: Why is reading the fine print wiser than choosing the cheapest ad?
qa.a: The fine print showed traps like a four-year exclusion and a low room-rent cap that the ad would never mention.

qa.q: How does Aditi see Sudha's table?
qa.a: Aditi is impressed, admitting the waiting period would have gone unnoticed, and asks to use the table too.
